requirements.requirement: Run /usr/local/bin/os-comparison-worker as a managed systemd service named inventory-worker on node1
requirements.summary: A systemd unit /etc/systemd/system/inventory-worker.service was created with ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/os-comparison-worker, then enabled and started via 'systemctl enable --now'. Post-start verification shows the unit loaded, enabled, and active (running), with the worker process (PID 2316) executing the binary. After a full node restart, the service remained active and enabled, and the worker process (PID 871) was running again, confirming the service is durably managed by systemd rather than a one-off process.

requirements.requirement: Service runs under a dedicated inventorysvc account
requirements.summary: A dedicated system account inventorysvc was created via 'useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /sbin/nologin' (after resolving a PATH/permission issue by using sudo and the full /usr/sbin/useradd path), confirmed with uid=997(inventorysvc). The systemd unit sets User=inventorysvc/Group=inventorysvc, and process listings both immediately after start and after a full reboot show the worker process owned by the inventorysvc account (not root).

overall_summary: Both material outcomes from the task contract are satisfied with direct evidence: inventory-worker.service is a real systemd unit running /usr/local/bin/os-comparison-worker under the dedicated inventorysvc system account, verified both immediately after setup and after a full node restart. Beyond the contract, the executor also completed the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol thoroughly: a healthy pre-restart baseline (boot_id 192f6cab..., service active/enabled) was captured, a restart was acknowledged and triggered, a brief connectivity gap was observed, and the node came back with a new boot_id (3bcc1bea...) and fully recovered service/account state. This sequence is cross-checked and consistent with the fixed after_prepare (192f6cab...) and after_executor (3bcc1bea...) boot-identity snapshots. Only a trivial leftover log file (/tmp/reboot.log) was left behind.
limitations: Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) in all three lifecycle snapshots, so native package consistency could not be verified as a cross-check, though this is unrelated to the executor's actions.
/tmp/reboot.log created during the restart trigger was not cleaned up; low-impact but technically unreverted residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace is clean: two initial useradd attempts (cmd-6a0acc23dd674c40, cmd-8b8f4841ea9a4ee6) failed outright (PATH issue, then permission denied) and made no state changes, then the corrected sudo invocation (cmd-587eba3e6e5842f8) succeeded — this is normal troubleshooting, not an unnecessary mutation, since nothing was left in a bad state. All other state-changing commands (account creation, unit file write, daemon-reload, enable+start, and the reboot trigger) map directly to the task outcome or to the provider-wide restart-evidence protocol. One minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log was created by redirecting 'shutdown -r now' output and was not cleaned up, visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot; it is a tiny, low-risk log artifact with no security or functional impact. No failed services, no unexpected listening sockets, and no damaged package state were observed in the after_executor snapshot (listening-socket differences are just PID churn from the reboot, not new exposure).
